## Research Process
The research process followed a structured, stage-based sequence, illustrated in @fig-rp-flowchart and described below.

**1. Scoping and literature review.** The project began by identifying the research gap through a systematic literature review of cetacean distribution research in the Western Mediterranean (Section [lit-review]). This established the absence of design-based survey within the BGTW and defined the central research question, aims, and objectives.

**2. Survey design.** A distance-sampling survey was designed to address this gap. Candidate designs were generated and evaluated in R using the `dssd` package, the study area was stratified, and field protocols, data sheets, and observer guidelines were prepared. A vessel-based pilot study was conducted to implement and improve the field protocol.  Ethical approval was obtained at this stage.

**3. Design revision.** When the intended vessel could not be deployed within the field-season window, the design was revised mid-project from vessel-based line transects to a land-based, point-transect design across the same strata (see @sec-revision).

**4. Data collection.** Systematic land-based observations were conducted from three vantage points, with opportunistic photographic identification collected alongside. Environmental conditions and effort were recorded for every watch.

**5. Data processing and quality control.** Field data sheets were imported through an automated cleaning pipeline in R (see @sec-pipeline), which applied validation checks and derived sighting positions from reticle readings and bearings.

**6. Analysis.** Processed data were analysed in stages: encounter-rate comparison, detection-function fitting and density estimation, kernel density estimation, and comparison against opportunistic OBIS records.

**7. Reporting.** Results were synthesised into this supplementary document and the accompanying journal article, with all analytical code version-controlled and publicly available ([GitHub](https://github.com/datsimon-design/Masters_Project)).

Although presented sequentially, the process was iterative: the analytical pipeline was developed in parallel with data collection so that analysis could begin immediately after fieldwork, and the mid-project design revision (step 3) fed back into data collection and analysis. This parallel working provided the schedule slack that absorbed the vessel delay without compromising delivery.

![Flowchart of the research process, from initial planning and survey design through data collection, analysis, and reporting of results.](/misc/research_process_flowchart.png){height=70% #fig-rp-flowchart}


A detailed Gantt chart was developed at the proposal stage to schedule work packages against the fixed submission timeline (@fig-gantt-planned). The schedule was deliberately layered, with the literature review, methods development, and analysis-pipeline preparation running in parallel with the field season rather than sequentially after it. This overlap was a deliberate risk-management measure, building slack into the timeline against the possibility of field-season disruption. That slack proved decisive: when vessel availability delayed the start of fieldwork, the realised schedule (@fig-gantt-actual) departed from the plan by only a single week, and because the analytical workflow was already in development the delay did not propagate into the downstream analysis or reporting phases. The close correspondence between the planned and realised timelines reflects both the layered design and the containment of the vessel delay to the data-collection phase.

![Planned project Gantt chart, developed at the proposal stage, showing the intended scheduling of work packages against the fixed submission timeline. Tasks were deliberately layered, with literature review, methods development, and analysis preparation running in parallel with the field season.](/misc/gannt_planned.png){#fig-gantt-planned}

![Realised project Gantt chart, showing the actual timeline. The one-week delay to fieldwork caused by vessel availability is the only substantive departure from the planned schedule (@fig-gantt-planned), and did not propagate into the analysis or reporting phases.](/misc/gannt_actual.png){#fig-gantt-actual}


## Data collection
### Underlying Principal - Distance Sampling
Distance sampling is a widely established and rigorously validated methodology for the systematic estimation of animal abundance and distribution [@bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015; @bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001]. The method is based on the principle that the probability of detecting an animal decreases with increasing distance from the observer, by modelling this detection probability, approximately unbiased estimates of population density can be derived under the method's assumptions [@bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015; @bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001; @thomasDistanceSoftwareDesign2010]. Since its formalisation, distance sampling has been successfully adapted across a broad range of terrestrial, aerial, and aquatic survey contexts, demonstrating considerable methodological flexibility [@dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008; @dickUsingDistanceSampling2011a; @bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015].

Within the field of marine mammal science, distance sampling has become one of the most frequently applied methods for estimating cetacean abundance and distribution [@dickUsingDistanceSampling2011a; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @raudinoAerialAbundanceEstimates2023], forming the basis of large-scale systematic surveys conducted by organisations including the `#gls("iwc")`{=typst}, `#gls("accobams")`{=typst} and `#gls("noaa")`{=typst} [@AbundanceCetaceansCalifornia; @macleodAbundanceAtlanticWhitesided2004; @stephanisSummerSpatialDistribution2008]. Shipboard line transect surveys, in particular, have been employed extensively to monitor cetacean populations across a range of geographic scales, from oceanic basins to coastal and riverine habitats [@AbundanceCetaceansCalifornia; @lerczakCalculatingSightingDistances1998; @dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008; @dickUsingDistanceSampling2011a; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @thomasDistanceSoftwareDesign2010]. 

<!-- Give a rational why the method was implemented like this -->
### Boat-based - Survey design
The study was originally designed as a vessel-based line-transect survey — the first dedicated systematic cetacean survey within the `#gls("bgtw")`{=typst} — following established distance-sampling methodology [@bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001; @thomasDesigningLineTransect2023]. Although logistical constraints ultimately required a shift to land-based sampling, the strata defined during this design were retained for the land-based survey, and the proposed design is therefore described here.

To meet the basic assumptions for a good survey design mentioned by Thomas et al. [-@thomasDesigningLineTransect2023] the starting point of the survey was chosen randomly using a random seed for every transect design within the `dssd` package [@marshallDssdDistanceSampling2025]. To minimise the time travelling between survey legs (off-effort time) an equal spaced zigzag design was chosen. The zigzag design was laid out so there are only a minimal number of apexes, to avoid biases caused by responsive movement of the species [@dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008].

To prevent the survey legs to spread, due to the shape of the survey area [@strindbergZigzagSurveyDesigns2004; @dawsonSmallboatSurveysCoastal2004; @dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008] the area was split into three strata (East, South and West, see @fig-area). Within those strata the zigzag design followed the longest axis of the area and as perpendicular to the coastline as possible, to increase the number of replicates [@strindbergZigzagSurveyDesigns2004; @dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008; @thomasDesigningLineTransect2023; @strindbergZigzagSurveyDesigns2004; @dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008]. The survey vessel followed this designed survey as closely as possible, while maintaining a speed of 10 knots to ensure even coverage and effort [@dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008]. A Garmin 78s GPS Device was used to record the vessel track and locations of the sightings.

![Sampling area divided in the three strata (East, South and West) in order to achieve effective transects. Zigzag transects are overlayed (orange) and follow the longest axis of the strata. The starting point of the transects will be shifted every survey.](/figures/region_transects.png){#fig-area}

To ensure standardised and reproducible data collection, all observers followed a set of survey guidelines prepared for this study (@app-protocol). These guidelines were designed both to standardise field practice across observers and to address the core assumptions of distance sampling, minimising the risk of their violation [@dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008]. They comprised four components. First, a scanning protocol, adapted from Dawson et al. [-@dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008], specifying search behaviour, sector coverage, and effort definitions designed to satisfy the assumptions of distance sampling as closely as field conditions allowed. Second, a data-recording protocol defining which variables were collected for each sighting and how they were to be entered, to ensure consistency across watches and observers. Third, a `#gls("pid")`{=typst} guide, adapted from Rosel et al. [-@roselPhotoidentificationCapturemarkrecaptureTechniques2011] and Karczmarski et al. [-@karczmarskiIndividualIdentificationPhotographic2022], setting out image-capture and quality criteria for opportunistic photo-ID. Fourth, a behavioural classification table, adapted from Neumann and Orams [-@neumannBehaviourEcologyCommon] and Hawkins and Gartside [-@hawkinsInteractiveBehavioursBottlenose2009], to standardise the assignment of behavioural states in the field. A corresponding checklist (@app-checklist) supported field preparation, data collection and the workflow in a whole. All fieldwork was conducted in accordance with ethical guidelines for marine mammal research [@wuersigMethodsPhotoidentificationSmall1990], ensuring minimal disturbance to the animals and their habitats.


By comparing systematic outputs against existing opportunistic datasets (OBIS, https://mapper.obis.org/), this study critically evaluated the relative value of each monitoring approach for informing conservation and management decisions in geographically bounded marine territories.



### Photo Identification (Photo-ID)
Alongside the systematic boat-based distance-sampling data, opportunistic photo identification data were collected, to further assess species composition and distribution within the `#gls("bgtw")`{=typst}. Small cetaceans, such as short-beaked common dolphins (*Delphinus delphis*), striped dolphins (*Stenella coeruleoalba*) and bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops truncatus*) are the most commonly encountered species in the `#gls("bgtw")`{=typst} [@canales-caceresDistributionBehaviourStriped2023; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @olaya-ponzonePhotoIdentificationCatalogueDelphinus2025; @olaya-ponzoneMixedspeciesDolphinGroups2025; @olaya-ponzoneSpatioTemporalPatternsLimited2026; @olaya-ponzoneVesselInducedBehavioural2025]. 
Because of the expected species in this region, the method to capture `#gls("pid")`{=typst} data was therefore adapted and applied to small cetaceans [@wuersigMethodsPhotoidentificationSmall1990; @roselPhotoidentificationCapturemarkrecaptureTechniques2011].

Individuals were identified from unique, naturally occurring markings on the dorsal fin, principally the shape of the trailing edge and the position and configuration of nicks, notches, and scars [@wuersigMethodsPhotoidentificationSmall1990; @roselPhotoidentificationCapturemarkrecaptureTechniques2011] (@fig-markings). Such markings, particularly nicks and notches to the fin edge, are acquired through the animal's life and are considered stable over periods of years, making them reliable features for longitudinal recognition [@roselPhotoidentificationCapturemarkrecaptureTechniques2011] (see [Appendix C](#app-photoid_sec) for examples). 

![Examples of natural dorsal-fin markings used for individual identification: edge nicks and notches (A), epibiont growth (B), and rake marks (C).](/misc/markings.png){#fig-markings}


Each usable image was graded for photographic quality (focus, exposure, angle, and the proportion of the fin visible) and each identified individual for distinctiveness, so that matches were based only on images of sufficient quality to minimise the risks of false-positive and false-negative identification [@karczmarskiIndividualIdentificationPhotographic2022]. Images were then compared against one another and against the developing catalogue to identify recaptures within the study period.

Images were captured using a Canon EOS R50 with a Canon 100–400 mm telephoto lens, following the `#gls("pid")`{=typst} protocol (@app-protocol) modified to incorporate `#gls("pid")`{=typst} best practices [@roselPhotoidentificationCapturemarkrecaptureTechniques2011; @karczmarskiIndividualIdentificationPhotographic2022]. Photo-ID records were organised, filtered, ranked, and matched across encounters using the DISCOVERY software [@chanApplicationMultispeciesPhotoID2022; @chanIndoPacificHumpbackDolphins2017; @chanUnknownComponentWellknown2022], which supports the creation and maintenance of individual identification catalogues. Photo-ID outputs are provided as supplementary material (@app-photoid).

### Design revision{#sec-revision}
The study was originally designed and proposed as a vessel-based line-transect survey . However, the intended university research vessel could not be launched within the field-season window, as arrangements for its transport and craning into the marina were not completed in time. Despite the university's repeated assertions, both in the project planning, the proposal phase and in subsequent updates, that the vessel would be made available, this has not been the case. In consultation with the project supervisor, continued delay was judged unfeasible given the fixed timeframe, and the survey was consequently revised to a land-based station design covering the same three strata.

This revision has two consequences for interpretation. First, the land-based stations sampled only part of the `#gls("bgtw")`{=typst}, so density and distribution estimates represent the surveyed sectors rather than the territory as a whole. Second, the change from randomly placed transects to fixed observation points alters the sampling geometry from line- to point-transect distance sampling, with implications addressed in the Discussion (see @sec-limits).


### Land-based Survey
Following the logistical constraints described above, land-based cetacean surveys represent a viable and cost-effective alternative to the more expensive vessel-based surveys. The utilisation of vantage points facilitates a better overview of the situation and as such an easier interpretation of the behaviour. The behaviour state was defined using an adaptation of Neumann and Orams [-@neumannBehaviourEcologyCommon] and Hawkins and Gartside [-@hawkinsInteractiveBehavioursBottlenose2009] (Travelling, Milling, Foraging, Socialising, and Resting) (@tbl-behave). In the context of behavioural studies, land-based surveys have been a particularly effective method of data collection, as they do not influence the behaviour of cetaceans or introduce bias via the survey vessel [@mannBehavioralSamplingMethods1999].


| **Behaviour State** | **Description** |
|:-- |:---------- |
| Travelling | Dolphins move in one defined direction and surface consistently. |
| Milling | Dolphins change swimming direction frequently but remain in the same general area. |
| Feeding/Foraging | Dolphins actively pursue prey or capture fish. Associated with deep diving, fast swimming; frequent direction changes and inconsistent breath-intervals. |
| Socialising | At least two dolphins make physical contact at the surface. Like chasing each other, body contact, petting or copulation. Often accompanied by breaching or other surface activities. |
| Resting | Dolphins stay close to the surface and to each other. They regularly surface at regular intervals and move only very slowly or do not move forward at all. |

: Definition table of behaviour states of dolphins adapted from Neumann and Orams (2005) and Hawkins and Gartside (2009). {#tbl-behave}


Surveys were conducted from three vantage points selected to cover the majority of the `#gls("bgtw")`{=typst}: Europa Point, Prince George, and Sandy Bay (@tbl-landspots, @fig-spots). Observers remained on-effort for 10-minute periods separated by 20-minute breaks, allowing observer rest and reducing double-counting by permitting animals to leave the surveyed area [@gutierrez-munozPatternsTrendsCetacean2021]. In total, 174 surveys (including pilot surveys) were conducted between the sunrise and sunset. Surveys were postponed when visibility was poor or sea state exceeded Beaufort 5.

| Europa Point | South | 36°06′33.48″ N | 5°20′44.34″ W | 18 | 060–220° | 5,654 m |

![Point of views of the three selected vantage points (Prince George (A), Sandy Bay (B) and Europa Point (C), facing left (a), right (b) and a wide shot of the spot (c). Overview of the area covered by each spots sector (D).](/figures/spots_comb.png){#fig-spots}

Observations were carried out both with the naked eye and using binoculars (Fujinon 7 × 50) using the continuous horizon scanning method [@mannBehavioralSamplingMethods1999]. When an observation was made, the time, number of reticles, horizontal bearing, species and group size were documented; the presence of birds or fish was also noted, where possible. Photographs were recorded opportunistically using a Canon EOS R50 camera  with a telephoto lens (Canon 100 – 400 mm) to support subsequent species confirmation and behavioural assessments.



## Data Cleaning and Quality Control{#sec-pipeline}
To streamline data handling and ensure reproducibility, a data-cleaning pipeline was implemented in R [@zotero-item-2907]. Raw field data sheets were imported automatically and passed through a sequence of quality-control checks before any downstream processing. These checks combined conditional validation of individual fields—verifying, for example, that reticle readings, bearings, group sizes, and environmental variables fell within permissible ranges and that categorical entries matched their controlled vocabularies. Using assertion-based stops (`stopifnot`-style guards) that halted execution when a record violated a predefined criterion. This fail-fast design ensured that data-entry errors were caught at the point of import rather than propagating silently into the analysis, so that any records requiring correction were flagged explicitly before proceeding (see code in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/datsimon-design/Masters_Project/blob/main/datacleaning.R) or in @app-QCinR). Once validated, custom functions derived sighting distances from the recorded reticle readings and bearings, and the resulting cleaned dataset was retained for subsequent analysis.


## Data Analysis
### Distance calculation
Radial distance to each sighting ($d$) was derived from reticle readings following the shore-based principle of Lerczak and Hobbs [-@lerczakCalculatingSightingDistances1998], adapted here to account for sea-surface curvature and, at the western station, for a coastline reference. The depression angle to a target at horizontal distance $d$ was modelled as

$$
\theta = \frac{h}{d} + \frac{d}{2R}
$$

where $h$ is the observer height and $R$ the Earth's radius (6,371 km); the second term corrects for the curvature of the sea surface between observer and target. The total depression angle to a sighting is the angle of the reference line ($\theta_{ref}$) plus the reticle angle,

$$
\theta = \theta_{ref} + rF,
$$

where $r$ is the number of reticles subtended between the sighting and the reference line and $F$ the instrument-specific reticle factor (0.005 for the Fujinon 7 × 50 FMTRC-SX binoculars used here). Distance was then recovered by inverting the quadratic:

$$
d = R\theta - \sqrt{(R\theta)^2 - 2Rh}.
$$

At the open-water stations (Europa Point, Sandy Bay), the reference line was the sea horizon, for which $\theta_{ref} = \sqrt{2h/R}$. Combined with the horizontal bearing, each distance was used to project the sighting location from the observer's position for mapping (see Supplementary Material).

Because of the enclosed nature of the western survey area (the Bay of Gibraltar), the far shore rather than the sea horizon was visible along most bearings from the Prince George station. The coastline sits closer than the true horizon and therefore at a greater angle of depression, so applying the horizon reference would overestimate sighting distances. For this station the reference distance ($d_{ref}$) was instead determined per bearing: using a detailed polygon of the bay's landmasses (including the detached mole off Algeciras, the first visible obstacle on some bearings), a ray was cast from the observation point along the recorded horizontal bearing, and the distance to the first intersection with land was taken as $d_{ref}$. The reference depression angle was then $\theta_{ref} = h/d_{ref} + d_{ref}/(2R)$, entering the same total-angle expression and inversion above. Bearings pointing out of the bay mouth, where no coastline was intersected, reverted to the horizon reference. Worked examples in R are provided in the Supplementary Material and repository ([GitHub](https://github.com/datsimon-design/Masters_Project)).

Following the calculations elaborated above a visual representation is provided here to better understand the principal of the distance calculation, the visualisation shows the simplified formula without the correction for the Earth's curvature ($d = \frac{h}{\tan(\theta)}$). The R code and analysis uses the corrected formula mentioned above. The observers height $h$ was adapted per spot and the angle $\theta$ was derived from the reticles inside the binoculars. The distance $d$ was then calculated using the formula above. A birds eye view shows how the location of a sighting can be calculated using the distance $d$ and the binocular bearing (@fig-inclinometer).

![Visual representation of the calculation of the distance used in the data cleaning pipeline. The observer height $h$ was adapted per spot and the angle $\theta$ was derived from the reticles inside the binoculars.](/misc/Inclinometer.png){#fig-inclinometer}


### Detection Function {#det-func}
The `Distance` package requires a flatfile format [@bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015] (@app-flat), the data from the effort and sighting logs were therefore first mutated and then joined, the effort was calculated by dividing the sector degrees by 360. The area for each wedge was calculated and added to the data frame. The truncation distance was determined separately for each sampling location based on the corresponding distribution of observed distances (see [Detection model fitting](#model_fit) for values). Detection functions were first fitted per station using the `ds` function, following a two-step procedure: candidate key functions (half-normal and hazard-rate) were compared by `#gls("aic")`{=typst}, goodness-of-fit test (`gof_ds`), and Q–Q plot, and the best-supported key function was then tested with candidate covariates (wave height, glare, sea state, and wind speed) to assess whether they improved fit. 

Because the per-station samples were insufficient to support stable detection functions [@bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015], a single pooled detection function was additionally fitted across all stations, following the same two-step procedure. For the pooled model, observation height was tested as an additional covariate alongside those above. The pooled detection function was used for the density estimates reported here, with per-station estimates retained for comparison. Density was estimated separately for groups and individuals.


### Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
`#gls("kde")`{=typst} is a well-established tool for describing the spatial distribution and relative abundance of cetaceans [@raymentKernelDensityEstimates2009; @milmannTemporalSpatialDistribution2017]. It was used here to describe the relative spatial distribution of cetaceans within the BGTW. The locations of all on-effort sightings—derived from reticle-based radial distances and compass bearings (see Calculation), were projected to UTM zone 30N so that smoothing was performed in metric units, and used as input to the kernel density estimation. A bivariate kernel density surface was computed in R using the `ks` package [@duongKsKernelSmoothing2005], with each sighting weighted by its group size so that the surface reflected the relative density of individuals rather than of sightings alone. The smoothing bandwidth was selected automatically using a plug-in bandwidth matrix [@duongPluginBandwidthMatrices2003], and density was evaluated over a 100 × 100 grid spanning the survey area. KDE is a well-established tool for describing the spatial distribution and relative abundance of cetaceans [@canales-caceresDistributionBehaviourStriped2023; @raymentKernelDensityEstimates2009; @milmannTemporalSpatialDistribution2017]. 

Because the resulting surface is a normalised probability density (integrating to one), it provides a descriptive, relative measure of spatial concentration, it was not corrected for observation effort or imperfect detection, which were instead accounted for separately through the distance-sampling density estimation ([Detection Function](#det-func)). The surface was visualised over the study area and overlaid with the observation stations and individual sightings to identify areas of elevated cetacean occurrence.

### Statistical Analysis
All statistical analyses were carried out in R [@zotero-item-2907]. `#gls("spue")`{=typst}, calculated as the number of sightings per on-effort scan, was strongly right-skewed and zero-inflated and did not meet the assumptions of parametric analysis of variance (normality of residuals and homogeneity of variance). A non-parametric approach was therefore adopted, with each on-effort scan treated as the sampling unit. Differences in `#gls("spue")`{=typst} among the three active observation stations (Europa, Sandy Bay and Prince George) were tested using a Kruskal–Wallis rank-sum test [@KruskalWallis1952]. Where the omnibus test was significant, pairwise differences were identified using Dunn's post-hoc test [@dunnMultipleComparisonsUsing1964], which operates on the pooled ranks of the Kruskal–Wallis test and accounts appropriately for tied values. P-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure [@benjaminiControllingFalseDiscovery1995].

### Comparison with opportunistic records
To evaluate the systematic survey against existing opportunistic data, occurrence records of *Delphinus delphis* were retrieved from the `#gls("obis")`{=typst} ([OBIS Mapper](https://mapper.obis.org/)) using the `robis` package [@provoostRobisOceanBiodiversity2022], constrained to a bounding box encompassing the study area (-5.438/-5.248; 36.05/36.195). Records lacking coordinates were excluded, and the remainder were projected to CRS 4326 and assigned to survey sectors by spatial intersection with the stratum polygons. The spatial distribution of opportunistic records was then compared with that of the systematic on-effort sightings, both visually (@fig-obis) and by tabulating record counts per sector (@tbl-obis_comp). Because opportunistic records carry no associated survey effort, the comparison was restricted to spatial coverage and was not interpreted in terms of relative abundance.

## Ethics statement
This study was carried out under the University of Gibraltar approval, Ethics ID: 259/2026/UniGib.


Abundance estimates are reported for the area covered by the survey at each station—that is, the density estimate scaled to the effectively surveyed area (the scanned sector out to the truncation distance) rather than to the full geographic extent of each stratum or the territory as a whole. This "covered-area" abundance [@buckland2001; @thomas2010] requires no extrapolation beyond the surveyed region and therefore does not depend on the assumption of randomised transect placement that underpins design-based extrapolation to a wider area [@buckland2015; @miller2019]. Because the fixed observation stations did not randomly sample the BGTW and cetacean density was strongly spatially structured, abundance was not extrapolated to the full territory; the estimates below quantify the number of animals estimated within the areas actually surveyed.
